transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-01 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Tom Rivers (Redwood SE), Sarah Kim (Atlas), Liam O'Connor (Atlas), Priya Desai (Atlas), James Wu (Atlas)
Shared: deck -> https://redwood.app/decks/hosted-chat-edu (shared by Maya), sandbox invite link -> https://console.redwood.dev/sandbox/atlas (shared by Tom)

Summary (auto): Educational session focusing on when to use streaming vs synchronous responses, parameter tuning basics (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry mapping strategies for hosted API, and mitigation patterns for partial responses. Action items and next steps captured.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you taking the time. We're gonna run through a short edu session — show the hosted chat API behaviors for streaming vs sync, go over how parameters affect tokenization and hallucination risk, and then map out retry strategies so you don't double-charge or re-run side effects.
[00:18] Sarah (Atlas): Thanks Maya, excited. Quick note — our traffic is mostly short customer-support snippets, average turn length 50 tokens, peaks to about 35 qps. We care a lot about latency under 200ms  p95 and cost.
[00:32] Tom (Redwood SE): Got it. That's actually a helpful profile. We'll show where streaming helps for perceived latency and where sync is simpler for idempotency. Also we'll cover the KV cache/prefix caching patterns — sometimes the transcript has KV cash in older notes — so heads up for the auto transcription typos.
[00:45] Liam (Atlas): Quick thing — we have an internal policy about E2E encryption and KMS integration, and audit logs are non-negotiable.
[00:51] Maya: Totally, we'll cover SSO, KMS options for Private, and audit logs in the console. For hosted we have envelope encryption and integrations with common KMS providers, and audit trails in Redwood Console (audit retention is configurable).
[01:05] Priya (Atlas): Who from Redwood usually owns the sandbox runs? We want a clean environment that mimics our traffic patterns.
[01:11] Tom: We can provision a dedicated sandbox project and seed it with your sample prompts and concurrency profile. That way we can run an apples-to-apples latency sweep. We'll also put a light canary policy in — canary traffic to a smaller model first.
[01:25] James (Atlas): When you say canary, are you doing A/B or full fallback? What's the behavior on capacity constraint?
[01:31] Tom: Good question. Hosted routing is policy-driven — you can route by latency SLO, cost band, region. If the primary model is saturated we automatically fallback to a compatible model variant (lower precision/quantized or smaller architecture). There's also an option for rate-limited queuing versus immediate fallback. We'll show a live example in the sandbox.
[01:50] Maya: Alright let's jump into the demo. Tom, do you want to open the calls in the console and show a streaming session vs a sync call?
[01:56] Tom: Yep. Sharing screen now. (screen share) So first, here's the Console -> Generations page. I'm going to run two requests — one streaming websocket and one synchronous REST.
[02:10] [02:10] Tom: Streaming demo (start): connecting via ws, sending initial system prompt, then user prompt: "Summarize the return policy in two bullets for a customer with order #1234." You'll see incremental tokens arrive.
[02:24] [02:24] (audio glitch)
[02:27] Tom: — sorry, little packet glitch there — but you can see the first token chunk arrives in ~120ms for this short prompt. The full response completed in 320ms.
[02:35] Sarah: So streaming gave perceived latency of first token ~120ms which is within our goal. What's the tradeoff in cost or complexity?
[02:42] Tom: Streaming per se doesn't change token cost — you still pay per token generated — but it increases connections and requires client handling for partial content, reconnects, and idempotency. If you need strict single side-effect per request semantics, sync with idempotency tokens is safer.
[02:58] Maya: We often recommend a mixed map: use streaming for UX-focused simple answers (support chat, search snippets), and use sync for operations that trigger external workflows (refunds, DB writes).
[03:12] Liam: About idempotency — what's the canonical approach? We have internal orchestration that will retry on 5xx.
[03:18] Tom: Use the Redwood request-id + idempotency token header. On the client side, tag requests that will cause side-effects and ensure orchestration checks the token before re-triggering. Also, for streaming if the client reconnects you can resume from a known token offset with the KV cache if you have session state — that's where prefix caching helps.
[03:36] Sarah: Are there built-in backoff policies? We want exponential backoff but also prefer jitter.
[03:42] Tom: Yes, the SDK offers recommended retry strategies with exponential backoff + jitter, and we expose circuit-breaker hooks in the Console so you can tune thresholds per-route.
[03:50] [03:50] (crosstalk)
[03:52] Maya: Let's flip to parameters briefly — temperature, top_p, max_tokens. We'll show how small changes change hallucination rate vs creativity. Tom, run three quick variations on the same prompt.
[04:05] Tom: Running variation A: temperature=0.0, top_p=1.0, max_tokens=60. Variation B: temp=0.7, top_p=0.95. Variation C: temp=0.2, top_p=0.8 plus more aggressive stop sequences.
[04:22] [04:22] Tom: Variation A returns deterministic concise answer — lower hallucination. B is more creative, tends to add inferred policy nuance that may not be accurate. C is a compromise. For your use case (support snippets) we usually recommend temp 0-0.2 with tight stop tokens.
[04:40] Priya: Can we enforce guardrails? We need to strip PII from answers or avoid certain topics.
[04:46] Maya: Redwood has response filters (safety layers) and you can add post-processing hooks in the Console. Also you can pin a safety model in the pipeline for an extra inference check — adds latency but increases safety. We'll include filter docs in the follow-up.
[05:02] Liam: Returning to failure modes — what happens on partial responses? Say the connection drops mid-stream?
[05:07] Tom: If connection drops, the SDK attempts reconnects for streaming; on reconnect you can request missing token ranges if you used the session KV cache. If not, best practice is to show partial answer to the user and offer a re-ask button which triggers a new request with idempotency token. For server-side retries we recommend mapping 5xx to a backoff+retry, but map 409/422 (client errors) to immediate fail.
[05:33] James: How do you avoid double-charging for multi-attempt workflows?
[05:36] Tom: Use idempotency tokens tied to your business transaction IDs. On the backend, Redwood exposes a request log in the Console and you can dedupe by idempotency token before performing side effects. We'll demo that in the sandbox.
[05:50] Sarah: Can you show an example of a retry map?
[05:54] Tom: Sure — I'll paste a simple mapping in chat: 
[05:58] Tom: "retry_map: {
  500: retry with backoff up to 3 attempts,
  502: immediate retry up to 2,
  503: queue and retry with exponential backoff,
  429: rate-limit backoff and failover to alternative model variant,
  4xx: fail and surface error to client }"
[06:19] Maya: Note that 429 handling is key — for hosted we often fallback to a cheaper model variant to preserve availability, or route to a cached answer if a prefix matches.
[06:30] Priya: Speaking of caching — does Redwood support prefix caching at request-time, like returning a cached vector or response?
[06:36] Tom: Yes, Console supports request-level caching, including prefix/KV cache for recurrent conversational context. It's configurable per-route with TTLs and size limits. Be mindful of stale info for sensitive data.
[06:48] Liam: For encryption / compliance: SOC 2, ISO? We need audit docs to pass legal review.
[06:54] Maya: We have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 documents; the Private deployment supports on-prem with HSM/KMS. We'll share the SOC 2 pack and details on audit log formats.
[07:07] Sarah: Any notes on data residency in EU? We need EU-only processing for some customers.
[07:12] Tom: Hosted supports region pinning to EU regions. For strict residency we recommend Redwood Private in a VPC or on-prem option.
[07:20] Maya: Back to UX tradeoffs — if you stream first token fast, you improve perceived latency but need client complexity. If you sync you avoid partial content but perceived latency is full response time. For chat, users prefer streaming for long answers.
[07:34] [07:34] (brief pause)
[07:36] Tom: I'd like to show how we instrument token-level latency in the Console so you can see p50/p95/p99 per route and per model. (shares chart) See here: a p95 jump around 1pm correlated with a model rollout. The Console ties that to rollouts and you can rollback or enable fallback automatically.
[07:56] Priya: Is there a way to automate model rollouts? We want canary 10% traffic for 24 hours then 50% then full.
[08:02] Tom: Yes, rollout policies are first-class. You can define percentage-based rollouts, canary windows, and automatic rollback on quality regressions detected by your eval hooks.
[08:12] Sarah: Talking about cost — if we fall back to a smaller model on spikes, how do we manage quality regression? We can't have wrong answers for support.
[08:21] Maya: For you, we'd recommend a tiered fallback: first try cached snippet, then quantized model with safety check, then fallback to human escalation. Redwood Optimize can generate model/quantization recommendations based on your prompts so we can tune for minimal quality loss.
[08:38] Liam: Will Optimize also give cost estimates?
[08:40] Tom: Yes, it forecasts token costs and suggests batching and caching knobs to reduce per-token spend. We'll include a sample Optimize report for your prompt set.
[08:49] [08:49] (audio artifact)
[08:52] Maya: Let's talk about rate control and throttling. We saw a scenario where spikes cause 429s — how do we protect downstream systems?
[08:59] Tom: Implement progressive throttling at the client with token bucket algorithm, honor 429 Retry-After headers, and use Redwood's per-route rate limits as a safety net. Also the Console can emit alerts when you hit burst thresholds.
[09:12] Sarah: For the sandbox run — can you mimic our spikes (35 qps) and token distribution?
[09:18] Tom: Yes, send the payloads and we'll configure the load generator. We'll also run a variant with streaming to measure first-token p50/p95.
[09:26] Priya: One more question on telemetry — can we get token-level cost broken down per conversation id?
[09:31] Maya: Yes, telemetry exposes token counts per request id and you can aggregate by conversation id in Analytics. That is how you attribute cost to product features.
[09:40] James: When we run POCs, how long before we can graduate to Dedicated? We need predictable throughput for peak Black Friday-like loads.
[09:47] Maya: Dedicated capacity requires a short sizing exercise; usually 2-4 weeks to provision depending on region and GPU type. For immediate needs, Reserved capacity or burst capacity options are available. We can include a dedicated sizing questionnaire in the follow-up.
[09:59] Tom: I'll note that Dedicated gives you predictable throughput and reduced noisy-neighbor variance, but at higher fixed cost. Hosted is great for elasticity and faster time-to-value.
[10:10] Sarah: Ok thanks — overall this is helpful. Could you capture the recommended parameter defaults for support snippets?
[10:15] Tom: Sure: temp 0.0–0.2, top_p 0.8–1.0, max_tokens 60, stop_sequences: ["\\n\\n", "—END—"], idempotency on side-effect APIs, streaming for long responses. We'll put that in a one-pager.
[10:30] Maya: Quick demo follow-up — I'm going to paste the pricing link and the SOC doc in chat. Also we'll schedule the sandbox walkthrough with Liam.
[10:38] (chat message posted: pricing link + SOC 2 pack)
[10:42] Sarah: Sounds good. Any final questions?
[10:45] Priya: Do you have a sample failure-runbook? We want concrete steps for SREs.
[10:50] Tom: Yes — we'll share a runbook that includes retry mapping, dedupe by idempotency tokens, and fallback ladder (cache -> smaller model -> human).
[10:59] Maya: Great. Recap of next steps: Maya will share pricing + SOC 2, Tom will run the sandbox latency sweep and schedule the deeper sandbox with Liam, Atlas will send sample prompts and QPS profile by Friday. Action items in the doc.
[11:15] Sarah: Thanks everyone. Meeting adjourned.

End of transcript.
